units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: We cannot say what Origen taught, but Augustine taught that the punishment of the lost has no end.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Augustine wrote that after the final judgment there are two kingdoms, and that the lost suffer in degrees.

Augustine wrote: “After the resurrection, when the final judgment of all has been completed, there will be two kingdoms. Each will have its own clear boundaries. One is Christ’s, the other the devil’s. One is made up of the good, the other of the bad. Both are made up of angels and human beings. The first will have no will to sin, and the second no power to sin. Neither will have any power to choose death. The first will live truly and happily in eternal life. The second will drag out a wretched existence in eternal death, without the power of dying. For both the life and the death will be without end. Among the first there will be degrees of happiness, one happier than another. Among the second there will be degrees of misery, one more bearable than another.”

units.label: paraphrase

They give a milder sense to sayings they think were meant more to frighten than to be taken as literally true.”

answers.addressed: How the church handled certificates of peace for the lapsed; nothing about Matthew 7.
answers.reason: It answers how the church handled certificates for the lapsed, not what was done with the saying in Matthew 7.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Among us, a name had to be set down before peace was asked for someone who had failed.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: That name was then examined before the whole congregation, with its judgment.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Cyprian wanted each certificate to name the person.

Cyprian wrote: “For I hear that some certificates are given in a way that says, ‘Let so-and-so be received into communion along with his own people.’ The martyrs never did this in any case. Such a vague and blind request will soon heap blame on us. For it opens a wide door to say, ‘So-and-so with his own people.’ Then twenty or thirty or more may be brought to us. They may be said to be the relatives, in-laws, freedmen and household of the man who received the certificate. For this reason I beg you to name in the certificate those whom you yourselves see and have known. Name those whose repentance you see is very near to full satisfaction. Then send us letters that agree with faith and discipline.”
Do you want us to go further into how we dealt with those who failed, or into the saying itself?

units.sentence: At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of communion for thinking differently.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: A century and a half later, Augustine argued at book length that the ruling of that council was wrong.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Augustine never put Cyprian outside our communion.

Augustine wrote: “The Winnower will come and divide the bad from the good. Then there will be a bodily separation too. A separation in spirit comes before it now. In heart, always keep apart from the bad. In body, stay joined with them for a time, but with caution. Yet do not neglect to correct your own people, those who in any way are in your care. Do it by warning, by teaching, by urging, or by threats.”
Is it the rite of the table you are asking about, or the standing we call communion?
